latest_post.title: Devon’s libraries are limited, plus a Sheffield switcheroo
latest_post.author: Ian Anstice / The Library Campaign

editorial.text: The name “Libraries Unlimited” for Devon’s non-profit trust is starting to look like a misnomer after it announced a plan to remove all its 19 current library supervisors and replace them with just 10 “library and community managers”. There’s been a lot of negative publicity about it in the local press this week and with good reason: :the council had only just agreed to invest £1 million in the service, for one thing, and the fact that some of these library supervisors look like they are downright loved by their local communities is another. And, to me anyway, the way the trust says this reduction will make things “more resilient” looks like a slap in the face for those whose jobs are currently in danger. Branch managers are the face of the library to their community, with a good one being an absolute dynamo. In reality, it’s hard to see how this move is anything but a cost-cutting measure. Avoid the temptation of management-speak and remember real people are involved – your colleagues for goodness sake – would be my advice to the trust’s management. Then on to Sheffield Central. This was my public library when I was doing a MA in Librarianship in the city and I remember it well. It was a beautiful building but even back then (1994) it was clear that it had limited funding, as there almost no new books on its shelves. News stories since 2010 suggest things have not improved much, with a 2017 article speculating on it being sold off to a Chinese-owned hotel chain and, six years later, reports that cracks in the building led to a three-metre “exclusion zone” around it. So this week’s news that the site of it and the town’s gallery being switched does not necessarily strike me as bad news, other than in terms of nostalgia and pondering about how this will affect its listed building status. It’s now down, as ever, to funding. Will the money come through? And if so will the city have the money to maintain the library sufficiently so as not need to sell or tape it off? The designs give some hope. There’s no cracks shown in any of them.
editorial.html:
The name “Libraries Unlimited” for Devon’s non-profit trust is starting to look like a misnomer after it announced a plan to remove all its 19 current library supervisors and replace them with just 10 “library and community managers”. There’s been a lot of negative publicity about it in the local press this week and with good reason: :the council had only just agreed to invest £1 million in the service, for one thing, and the fact that some of these library supervisors look like they are downright loved by their local communities is another. And, to me anyway, the way the trust says this reduction will make things “more resilient” looks like a slap in the face for those whose jobs are currently in danger. Branch managers are the face of the library to their community, with a good one being an absolute dynamo. In reality, it’s hard to see how this move is anything but a cost-cutting measure. Avoid the temptation of management-speak and remember real people are involved – your colleagues for goodness sake – would be my advice to the trust’s management.

Then on to Sheffield Central. This was my public library when I was doing a MA in Librarianship in the city and I remember it well. It was a beautiful building but even back then (1994) it was clear that it had limited funding, as there almost no new books on its shelves. News stories since 2010 suggest things have not improved much, with a 2017 article speculating on it being sold off to a Chinese-owned hotel chain and, six years later, reports that cracks in the building led to a three-metre “exclusion zone” around it. So this week’s news that the site of it and the town’s gallery being switched does not necessarily strike me as bad news, other than in terms of nostalgia and pondering about how this will affect its listed building status. It’s now down, as ever, to funding. Will the money come through? And if so will the city have the money to maintain the library sufficiently so as not need to sell or tape it off? The designs give some hope. There’s no cracks shown in any of them.

stories.text: Silence speaks volumes for the future of Helensburgh’s library – Lochside Press. “It is now 634 days since Helensburgh Library moved into Hermitage Park Pavilion (above); what was supposed to be a temporary arrangement must not be allowed to become permanent by default. The library moved in February 2025 to make way for a temporary gym at its premises in West King Street, following the damage caused to Helensburgh Leisure Centre by Storm Eowyn. There were understandable reasons for finding emergency accommodation for both services. That’s a question which Argyll and Bute Council is notably refusing to answer, while LiveArgyll remains as secretive as ever – no minutes or agendas of its meetings have been published since February 2025.”

stories.text: Sutton Coldfield library visitor numbers rise in first year under Town Council – Greater Birmingham Chambers of Commerce. “Royal Sutton Coldfield Town Council took over the library and community centre service at Mere Green, Walmley and Boldmere on 1 November 2025. Twelve months on, the council says all three sites have seen more people visiting the libraries and attending events and user groups. Library opening hours have been extended at all three sites, so one of the town’s libraries is now open every day from Monday to Saturday. More than 800 children in Sutton Coldfield completed this year’s free Summer Reading Challenge, up 48 per cent on last year.”

stories.entity_raw: Bridgend – Awen launches Baby Milestone Cards to celebrate the National Year of Reading
stories.text: Press release. “The beautifully illustrated cards feature a series of milestones including becoming a library member, borrowing a first library book and attending a Bounce and Rhyme session for the first time. Each card includes space to record the date and recognise the achievement. The cards are themes around some of Wales’s native wildlife, including Atlantic puffins and grey seals, red squirrels, bottlenose dolphins, Eurasian beavers and red kites, helping young families discover more about Welsh nature while creating lasting memories.”

Elsewhere, bookstores, public reading rooms, and literary gatherings have helped establish a cultural scene that extends beyond the city’s best-known tourist attractions. That investment has particular significance in a place that endured decades of violence and has spent years expanding access to education and public spaces.”

stories.text: Would you pay €30 for a library card? – Yle. “The Finance Ministry has put forward more than 100 proposals for spending cuts and tax hikes that it says could help the next government balance the economy. One of them is to introduce a charge for adult library cards. In its report, the ministry suggests an annual ‘reasonable fee’ of around 30 euros per card. It estimates this could raise about 36 million euros a year for the state. Library cards for public libraries are free. The principle is that everyone should be able to access basic services at no cost. Päivi H. Jokitalo, a freelance librarian and reading advocate, pointed out that free access is a statutory right in Finland. The country’s first library act, passed in 1928, states that library use must be free for all.”

stories.text: As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards – NPR. “Data shared with NPR by several of the largest public library systems in the U.S. show recent upticks in cardholder membership, circulation and event attendance. Librarians say part of that can be attributed to the rising cost of living — and the growing recognition that libraries’ resources extend far beyond physical books.” Disaster aid has become a political lottery – libraries, schools and places of worship are stepping into the breach – The Conversation. “The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades.” … and tend to do so only in Republican states … “Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, up 8.2% from 2022. Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan.”

These trailblazing editions are planned to release through top library partners, bringing these enchanting editions to even more people, through participating public libraries around the globe.” [Some news sources say these will be free for public libraries but this, the original article, does not explicitly say this. It reads that they’re free for the public as long as the libraries pay for them – Ed.]

stories.text: IFLA. 9-13 August 2027, London. “First up: read the Welcome Message from the UK National Committee, the outline of the Congress days, registration rates, and information on the venue and location—all linked in the page header above. Please be aware that the IFLA WLIC 2027 website is a work in progress that will grow and expand as more information is added over the coming months. London 2027 will be a special congress to launch IFLA’s 100th anniversary celebrations. But even if such a big birthday would suggest particular emphasis on our past, the congress theme of “Knowledge Powering Futures” will instead lead delegates from around the world into discussions about the evolution of our field and our role in shaping it” see also Call for WLIC 2027 Volunteers opens – IFLA. “If you have never attended a WLIC, volunteering can be your entry point to international librarianship and the world of IFLA.”
